questions.title: True statement about the clavicle
questions.question: Regarding the clavicle, which is true?

options.A: Trapezius muscle is attached to its medial 2/3
options.B: Pectoralis major is attached to its medial half
options.C: When fractured, its lateral third is elevated by sternomastoid muscle
options.D: It articulates with the coracoid process of the scapula

explanations.A: Incorrect. Trapezius attaches to the posterior border of the clavicle's lateral one-third, not its medial two-thirds.
explanations.B: Correct. Pectoralis major's clavicular head attaches along the anterior border and superior surface of roughly the medial half of the clavicle. This is the mirror image of trapezius's lateral-third attachment on the posterior border. It is one of the two large muscles that anchor onto the shaft itself rather than an end or a ligament.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sternomastoid attaches to the medial fragment, which it pulls upward — the lateral fragment is the one displaced, and it moves downward under the limb's weight, not upward.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The clavicle articulates only with the manubrium sterni and the acromion; the coracoid process is tethered to it only indirectly by the coracoclavicular ligament, not a true joint.

questions.learning_objective: State which named surface of the clavicle pectoralis major attaches to, and rule out the coracoid process as a clavicular articulation.

questions.title: Structure attached to the lateral one-third of the clavicle
questions.question: Which structure is attached to the lateral 1/3 of the clavicle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Subclavius occupies the subclavian groove on the inferior surface of the clavicle's middle third, not the lateral third.
explanations.B: Correct. Deltoid arises from the anterior border and superior surface of the lateral one-third of the clavicle, making it the odd one out among this group of medial/middle-third structures. This origin is continuous with deltoid's other origins from the acromion and scapular spine, together forming its characteristic curved line of origin. It is also the only structure in this list that is not confined to the clavicle's inferior surface.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The costoclavicular ligament attaches to the costal tuberosity on the inferior surface of the medial end of the clavicle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sternocleidomastoid attaches to the superior surface of the medial end of the clavicle, near the sternoclavicular joint.

questions.learning_objective: Name deltoid as the structure attached to the lateral one-third of the clavicle.

questions.title: Exception among inferior-surface clavicular attachments
questions.question: The inferior surface of the clavicle gives attachment to all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct. Deltoid attaches to the anterior border and superior surface of the clavicle's lateral third, not the inferior surface, which is why it is the exception among this group. Subclavius, and the costoclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments, all attach to the inferior surface instead, at the middle third, medial end and lateral end respectively.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Subclavius occupies the subclavian groove on the inferior surface of the middle third.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The costoclavicular ligament attaches to the costal tuberosity on the inferior surface of the medial end.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The coracoclavicular ligament attaches to the conoid tubercle and trapezoid line on the inferior surface of the lateral end.

questions.learning_objective: Identify deltoid as the one attachment in this group that is not on the clavicle's inferior surface.

questions.title: The earliest bone to ossify
questions.question: The earliest bone to ossify is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The radius begins ossifying later, in the diaphysis around the eighth embryonic week.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ulna's diaphysis begins ossifying at a similar, later stage than the clavicle.
explanations.C: Correct. The clavicle is the first bone in the body to begin ossifying, intramembranously, in the sixth embryonic week — even though, paradoxically, its medial epiphysis is the last of any bone to fuse, not completing until the mid-20s. This makes the clavicle a useful marker in forensic and developmental age estimation at both ends of life. Its early, intramembranous start (rather than the cartilage-model route most long bones use) is the specific fact this item tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The humerus begins ossifying later than the clavicle and by the more typical cartilage-model (endochondral) route.

questions.learning_objective: State that the clavicle is the first bone in the body to begin ossifying.

questions.title: Exception among medial-border-of-the-scapula attachments
questions.question: One of the following is NOT attached to the medial border of the scapula:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Levator scapulae attaches near the superior angle and the adjoining upper medial border.
explanations.B: Correct. Teres minor attaches to the lateral (axillary) border of the scapula, not the medial border — grouping it instead with teres major, which shares that lateral-border attachment. Levator scapulae, both rhomboids and serratus anterior all attach along the medial border instead, so teres minor is the one exception in this list. This medial-versus-lateral border distinction is a common source of confusion because both teres muscles sound alike.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Serratus anterior inserts along the whole costal surface of the medial border.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Rhomboid minor attaches to the medial border above the root of the scapular spine.

questions.learning_objective: Identify teres minor as attaching to the lateral, not medial, border of the scapula.

questions.title: Muscle attached to the coracoid process
questions.question: The coracoid process gives attachment to the ... muscle.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle, above the glenoid rim, not the coracoid process.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deltoid arises from the clavicle, acromion and scapular spine, not the coracoid process.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The long head of triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle, below the glenoid rim, not the coracoid process.
explanations.D: Correct. Pectoralis minor inserts on the tip of the coracoid process. The coracoid process's apex also gives origin to the conjoint tendon of coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps, but among the four options offered here only pectoralis minor is listed. Remembering that the long and short heads of biceps take different origins (supraglenoid tubercle versus coracoid) is the key discrimination this item is testing.

questions.learning_objective: Name pectoralis minor as attaching to the coracoid process, distinguishing it from the long heads of biceps and triceps.

questions.title: Exception among muscles attached to the scapula
questions.question: All of the following are attached to the scapula EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Deltoid arises from the scapular spine and acromion.
explanations.B: Correct. Pectoralis major attaches only to the clavicle, sternum and upper costal cartilages on its origin side, and to the humerus on its insertion side — it never touches the scapula at all, unlike deltoid, trapezius and serratus anterior, which all do. This is a useful discriminator because pectoralis major is so often grouped with the other large shoulder muscles in questions about the scapula. Its close neighbour pectoralis minor, by contrast, does reach the scapula, inserting on the coracoid process — a distinction worth keeping straight.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Serratus anterior inserts along the whole costal surface of the medial border.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Trapezius inserts on the scapular spine and acromion.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that pectoralis major has no attachment to the scapula, unlike deltoid, trapezius and serratus anterior.

questions.title: Lateral continuation of the spine of the scapula
questions.question: The spine of the scapula is continuous laterally as the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inferior angle is the scapula's lowest point, unrelated to the spine's lateral course.
explanations.B: Correct. The scapular spine runs across the posterior surface and, at its lateral end, is continuous with the acromion process, which overhangs the shoulder joint and articulates with the clavicle. Both deltoid and trapezius attach around this spine-to-acromion continuation, which is why the two muscles appear to meet in a single curved line when the back is inspected. This continuity is what makes the acromion easily palpable as the bony point of the shoulder.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The supraglenoid tubercle sits above the glenoid cavity on the scapula's neck, not at the end of the spine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The coracoid process projects from the scapula's neck anteriorly, a separate projection from the spine.

questions.learning_objective: State that the scapular spine continues laterally as the acromion process.

questions.title: Displacement of the lateral fragment in a clavicle fracture
questions.question: A 37-year-old female patient has a fracture of the clavicle at the junction between its medial 2/3 and lateral 1/3. The lateral portion of the fractured clavicle is displaced downward by which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. The lateral fragment carries the weight of the entire upper limb hanging from it, and this weight is what pulls it downward, forward and medially; pectoralis major assists by pulling it medially, but the dominant force named in this option — the limb's own weight — is the one the bank's key credits. Trapezius remains attached to the lateral fragment but is too weak against that dead weight to hold it up, which is exactly why the shoulder drops rather than staying level.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deltoid arises from the lateral fragment itself and does not act to displace it; it is pectoralis major, not deltoid, that contributes an additional medializing pull.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pectoralis minor attaches to the coracoid process of the scapula, not to the clavicle, and plays no part in clavicular fragment displacement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Trapezius is attached to the lateral fragment but is too weak to prevent — let alone cause — its downward drop; pectoralis minor is not attached to the clavicle at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that the weight of the upper limb (assisted by pectoralis major) displaces the lateral fragment of a fractured clavicle downward, and that trapezius cannot prevent this.

questions.title: Artery injured with a bleeding surgical-neck fracture
questions.question: A 10-year-old boy falls off his bike and has difficulty moving his shoulder. His radiograph and angiograph reveal a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus and bleeding from the point of the fracture. This accident most likely leads to damage to which artery?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The axillary artery lies well proximal to the surgical neck, ending at the lower border of teres major before the arm even begins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The profunda brachii artery runs in the spiral groove of the humeral shaft with the radial nerve, a more distal and posterior relation than the surgical neck.
explanations.C: Correct. The posterior circumflex humeral artery winds around the surgical neck of the humerus together with the axillary nerve, passing through the quadrangular space, which is exactly why a surgical-neck fracture at this level threatens both structures together. The anterior circumflex humeral artery also crosses the surgical neck anteriorly, but the angiographic bleeding point described here, at the point of fracture, is classically attributed to the posterior vessel travelling with the nerve. This pairing of the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery at the surgical neck is a frequently tested clinical correlation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior ulnar collateral artery runs with the ulnar nerve much further distally, around the elbow, not at the surgical neck of the humerus.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the posterior circumflex humeral artery as the vessel at risk, alongside the axillary nerve, in a surgical-neck humeral fracture.
